newsitem.title: UK: British mercenary says he was betrayed in PNG.
newsitem.headline: British mercenary says he was betrayed in PNG.

text.p: A British mercenary who led 65 soldiers to help put down an uprising in Papua New Guinea said on Thursday he felt betrayed by the South Pacific nation's army chief who had been in on the operation from the start.
Former British army colonel Tim Spicer also related how he was threatened with death by rebel soldiers who held a loaded gun to his head while he was in detention after his operation collapsed.

Spicer said Papua New Guinea (PNG) army chief Jerry Singirok, sacked last month, had negotiated details of a $36 million contact with Sandline International, Spicer's London-based "military consultancy", but later repudiated the deal.

The deal, under which Sandline would supply troops, weapons and helicopters to help the PNG government crush the uprising on the copper-rich island of Bougainville, fell apart after its terms were leaked to the press last month.
Spicer, 44, was held in PNG on firearms charges but was allowed to return to London after these were dropped.
Singirok was sacked after he sparked a crisis in PNG by demanding the resignation of the then Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan over plans to use the mercenaries in Bougainville.
Spicer said one of his colleagues had been told by Singirok that the Sandline contract was a perfect excuse for a constitutional crisis.
"I suppose I do feel betrayed," Spicer told a news conference on his return to London. "I feel let down by him. I think his behaviour was very peculiar."

Spicer spent more than 20 years in the British army, serving in the Falklands and Gulf wars and in Northern Ireland. He was the United Nations military media spokesman in Sarajevo in 1994, when he served under Britain's General Sir Michael Rose.
Spicer said his firm had been paid $18 million of the contract and negotiations were underway to recover the rest.
He conceded that the ignominious collapse of the contract had cast a shadow over Sandline's future prospects in the "military consultancy" business.
"I think it is very unfortunate the way it has turned out for us and for the government and people of Papua New Guinea. I don't think it has been a roaring success," Spicer said.
"I think it will give us a number of difficulties if I'm being honest."

Spicer was keen to reject any suggestions that his mercenary force had been called in to do the PNG government's "dirty work". His men were not "Dogs of War", but professional military men who offered a service to governments which needed it.
Spicer said that after his detention by rebel elements of the PNG defence force, he had been threatened with death on several occasions.
"An automatic pistol was put against my forehead and I was told that if I didn't cooperate I would be shot," he said.
